# RL training run diagnosis

Review the staged post-training experiment and determine whether it is healthy
or unhealthy. Treat the workspace as a historical snapshot: inspect its source,
effective configuration, launch scripts, data processing, reward logic, logs,
tracked metrics, and frozen evaluation evidence. Do not assume that an unusual
setting or implementation is causal without connecting it to observed behavior.

Use held-out evaluation evidence together with rollout, truncation, runtime,
optimization, and training signals. Training reward alone does not establish
held-out health. A truncated log is not by itself proof of a defect.

Do not launch a full training run, use the network, or modify the historical
snapshot. The dataset, held-out set, model, training-step budget, and evaluation
interval are fixed.

## Deliverable

Write one concise UTF-8 diagnosis to:

```text
$AUTORLBENCH_RESULTS/agent_answer.md
```

State the verdict, identify the concrete root cause or causes, and explain the
causal chain using specific workspace evidence. Distinguish root causes from
symptoms. Do not propose or implement a fix, and do not write other deliverable
files.
I'll systematically investigate this training run. Let me start by exploring the workspace structure and understanding the experiment setup.

def reverser(sentence):

    words_with_punctuation = punctuation_and_spaces = list(sentence)

29	def _score_timeout(seconds: Optional[float]):
30	    """Raise ``TimeoutError`` if the wrapped block runs longer than ``seconds``.
31	
32	    A single ``compute_score`` call on a pathological model output (e.g. a long,
33	    degenerate RL rollout that triggers catastrophic regex backtracking or a slow
34	    symbolic comparison) can run for a very long time. Because ``NaiveRewardManager``
35	    scores samples serially in the driver process, one such call blocks the entire
36	    training loop. This guard bounds the wall-clock time of each call.

import signal
from collections import defaultdict
from contextlib import contextmanager
from typing import Any, Optional

import torch

from verl import DataProto
from verl.utils.reward_score import default_compute_score
from verl.workers.reward_manager import register
from verl.workers.reward_manager.abstract import AbstractRewardManager


@contextmanager
def _score_timeout(seconds: Optional[float]):
    """Raise ``TimeoutError`` if the wrapped block runs longer than ``seconds``.

    A single ``compute_score`` call on a pathological model output (e.g. a long,
    degenerate RL rollout that triggers catastrophic regex backtracking or a slow
    symbolic comparison) can run for a very long time. Because ``NaiveRewardManager``
    scores samples serially in the driver process, one such call blocks the entire
    training loop. This guard bounds the wall-clock time of each call.

    Implemented with ``SIGALRM``, so it only takes effect on the main thread. If a
    handler cannot be installed (e.g. called from a non-main thread), it degrades to
    a no-op so reward computation still runs -- just without the timeout.
    """
    if not seconds or seconds <= 0:
        yield
        return

    def _handler(signum, frame):
        raise TimeoutError(f"compute_score timed out after {seconds}s")

    try:
        old_handler = signal.signal(signal.SIGALRM, _handler)
    except ValueError:
        # Not in the main thread -> SIGALRM is unavailable; run without a timeout.
        yield
        return

    signal.setitimer(signal.ITIMER_REAL, seconds)
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        signal.setitimer(signal.ITIMER_REAL, 0)
        signal.signal(signal.SIGALRM, old_handler)


@register("naive")
class NaiveRewardManager(AbstractRewardManager):
    """The reward manager."""

    def __init__(
        self, tokenizer, num_examine, compute_score=None, reward_fn_key="data_source", compute_score_timeout=None
    ) -> None:
        """
        Initialize the NaiveRewardManager instance.

        Args:
            tokenizer: The tokenizer used to decode token IDs into text.
            num_examine: The number of batches of decoded responses to print to the console for debugging purpose.
            compute_score: A function to compute the reward score. If None, `default_compute_score` will be used.
            reward_fn_key: The key used to access the data source in the non-tensor batch data. Defaults to
                "data_source".
            compute_score_timeout: Optional per-sample timeout (in seconds) for `compute_score`. If set, a single
                scoring call that exceeds this limit is aborted, assigned a reward of 0.0, and training continues,
                instead of blocking the whole loop. Defaults to None (no timeout, unchanged behavior).
        """
        self.tokenizer = tokenizer  # Store the tokenizer for decoding token IDs
        self.num_examine = num_examine  # the number of batches of decoded responses to print to the console
        self.compute_score = compute_score or default_compute_score
        self.reward_fn_key = reward_fn_key  # Store the key for accessing the data source
        self.compute_score_timeout = compute_score_timeout  # per-sample timeout (seconds) for compute_score

requires-python = ">=3.10"

# Note: While the formatter will attempt to format lines such that they remain within the line-length,

line-length = 120
exclude = ["scripts/legacy_model_merger.py"]

[tool.ruff.lint]
isort = {known-first-party = ["verl"]}
# c.f. https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/ce8d6b75fc0586045df75ee1568a5b5f9957251b/pyproject.toml
select = [
    # pycodestyle
    "E",
    # Pyflakes
    "F",
    # pyupgrade
    "UP",
    # flake8-bugbear
    "B",

"verl.trainer.ppo.reward",

]

[tool.setuptools.dynamic]
version = {file = "verl/version/version"}

[tool.setuptools.package-dir]
"" = "."

[tool.setuptools.package-data]
verl = [
  "version/*",
  "trainer/config/*.yaml",
  "trainer/config/*/*.yaml",
  "experimental/*/config/*.yaml",
]

# Diagnosis: Unhealthy

**Verdict:** The GRPO post-training run is **unhealthy**. Held-out validation accuracy
(`val-core/taco/acc/mean@1`) shows no improvement over training and in fact declined
from the zero-shot baseline.

# Diagnosis: Unhealthy

**Verdict:** The GRPO post-training run is **unhealthy**. Held-out validation accuracy
(`val-core/taco/acc/mean@1`) shows no improvement over training and in fact declined
from the zero-shot baseline.

## Root cause

**The binary (all-or-nothing) reward scoring function on the TACO code-generation
dataset provides an extremely sparse learning signal that is too weak to drive
meaningful improvement at the given step budget, batch size, and learning rate.**

## Causal chain

### 1. Binary reward collapses the per-sample signal

The custom reward function at `verl/utils/reward_score/taco.py:162` returns
`score = binary`, where `binary = 1.0` only when **every** hidden test case passes
and `0.0` otherwise. The average test case has many test assertions (the held-out
set contains problems with up to 275 tests per sample, as seen in the step-0
validation log line `n_pass/n_tests=0/275`). A model output that passes 273/275
tests receives zero reward — indistinguishable from a completely broken submission.

### 2. Low initial accuracy means most rollouts receive zero reward

- Initial validation accuracy (step 0, before training): **7.61%**
- Final validation accuracy (step 250): **5.43%**
- Training reward (`critic/score/mean`) at step 283: **7.03%**

At the initial accuracy level, proposed by the zero-shot base model `Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct`,
fewer than 1 in 13 rollouts earns a non-zero reward. With `rollout_n=8` samples per
prompt, the expected number of positive rewards in a mini-batch of 16 prompts is
roughly `16 × 8 × 0.076 = 9.7` out of 128 rollouts.

### 3. GRPO advantage normalization is dominated by noise

GRPO computes advantages by normalizing scores within each prompt group
(`norm_adv_by_std_in_grpo=True`). When most prompts receive zero rewards across all
8 rollouts, the advantage for that prompt group is a vector of zeros (no signal).
When a single rollout in a group gets a non-zero reward, the advantage signal is
driven by a single per-prompt outlier — the resulting updates are high-variance and
provide no reliable gradient direction.

Evidence: the logged advantages at step 283 have `critic/advantages/mean ≈ 0`,
confirming most rollouts sit near zero advantage. The `actor/pg_loss` hovers near
zero (-2.8e-5 to +5.2e-3) throughout training, and `actor/pg_clipfrac = 0.0` at
every logged step, indicating the policy gradient never produces meaningful updates.

### 4. KL divergence from reference stays near zero

`rollout_corr/kl ≈ 0.0007` throughout training, and `actor/ppo_kl = 0.0`. The
model barely moves from its initialization — the policy is not learning because
the loss landscape provides no usable gradient.

### 5. Training terminated early at step 284 (71% of budget)

The run logged its last step at step 284 (`wandb-summary.json` `_step=283`, log
shows step 284 entry) out of the 400-step budget — consistent with a run that was
stopped or timed out. But this is a symptom, not the cause: the dead gradient
meant the remaining 116 steps would not have rescued the run.

### 6. Pass rate confirms the model never improved code quality

`val-aux/taco/pass_rate/mean@1` (fraction of individual test cases passed)
oscillated between 0.176 and 0.226 across all validation checkpoints with no trend.
The model's ability to write correct code was flat from start to finish.

## Why this is a design defect and not just a hard problem

A binary `compute_score` is appropriate only when the base policy already achieves
a non-trivial success rate (ideally >30–50%) or when the rollout count per prompt
is very large (>>8) so that at least one non-zero reward per group is likely. For
this model–dataset pair (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on TACO with ~7.6% zero-shot
accuracy), the dense `pass_rate` score already computed inside `taco.py` would
provide a far more usable learning signal. The code at lines 164–168 explicitly
chooses `binary` over `pass_rate` as the `score` — this is the single decision
blocking learning.

## Supporting evidence

| Signal | Value | Interpretation |
|--------|-------|----------------|
| `val-core/taco/acc/mean@1` (step 0) | 0.0761 | Zero-shot baseline |
| `val-core/taco/acc/mean@1` (step 250) | 0.0543 | Degraded from baseline |
| `critic/score/mean` (step 283) | 0.0703 | Training reward ≈ 7% |
| `actor/pg_loss` (step 283) | -2.8e-5 | Negligible policy gradient |
| `actor/pg_clipfrac` (all steps) | 0.0 | No clipping — no learning happening |
| `rollout_corr/kl` (all steps) | ~0.0007 | Model barely moved from reference |
| `val-aux/taco/pass_rate/mean@1` (all steps) | 0.18–0.23 | No improvement trend |
| Rollout configuration | `n=8, batch=16` | 128 rollouts/step, ~10 positive on average |
| Runtime | ~7.95 hours, 284 steps | Run terminated before the 400-step budget |

The diagnosis has been written to `/logs/artifacts/agent_answer.md`. Here's a summary:

## Verdict: **Unhealthy**

The GRPO post-training run on TACO code generation with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct is unhealthy. Held-out validation accuracy declined from 7.61% at initialization to 5.43% at the last validation checkpoint (step 250), with zero improvement trend across any metric.

## Root Cause

The `compute_score` function in `verl/utils/reward_score/taco.py:164` uses a **binary (all-or-nothing) reward**: `score = binary` where `binary = 1.0` only when every hidden test case passes and `0.0` otherwise. With the base model achieving only ~7.6% accuracy, roughly 92% of all 128 rollouts per step receive zero reward. GRPO advantage normalization within each prompt group collapses to noise when most groups have all-zero scores, and the policy gradient (`actor/pg_loss ≈ -2.8e-5`) is effectively dead — confirmed by `actor/pg_clipfrac = 0.0` at every step (no clipping because no meaningful gradient exists) and `rollout_corr/kl ≈ 0.0007` (model hasn't moved from the reference).

The `pass_rate` score (fraction of individual test cases passed) is already computed inside `taco.py` but deliberately discarded in favor of the binary score. For a model with ~7.6% zero-shot accuracy on a hard code-generation benchmark, this sparse binary reward is fundame
